column3: A lakeside park in Hefei honoring Judge Bao, the incorruptible official of the Song dynasty who became China's best-loved symbol of fair justice in stories and operas.
A water town of narrow stone lanes, arched bridges and Ming and Qing houses, where boats still drift past old shopfronts.
The province's main museum, tracing Anhui from ancient bronzes to the culture of the Hui merchants, with a fine collection of local arts and crafts.
One of China's five great freshwater lakes, a wide blue sheet beside Hefei, ringed with wetlands, fishing villages and lakeside walks.
Hefei's own roast duck, made with a sweet, savory glaze and a crackling skin that locals eat with a bowl of hot rice.
Thin, chewy rice-flour dumplings from Sanhe, folded around a juicy filling of pork and vegetables and a classic of the water town.
In summer, Hefei fills its streets with red crayfish stir-fried in garlic, chili and spices, eaten by hand with a cold beer.
A hearty hotchpotch of meatballs, egg dumplings and more, named for the Qing statesman Li Hongzhang, who came from the Hefei area.
Sheer granite peaks, pines clinging to the cliffs and seas of drifting cloud. Huangshan has inspired Chinese ink painters for centuries and is a UNESCO World Heritage Site.
A famous pine reaching out one arm over the cliff as if to welcome visitors, it is one of the best-known trees in China.
One of the main summits of Huangshan, popular for its wide views over the peaks and for watching the sun rise through the clouds.
The tallest peak of Huangshan, rising above the sea of cloud like the petals of a lotus. The final climb is steep and often crowded.
An old village of white walls, dark roofs and carved stone gateways, built by wealthy merchants. Together with Hongcun it is a UNESCO World Heritage Site.
A village laid out around a moon-shaped pond, with a clever water channel running past every house. Its reflections of white walls and ink-dark roofs look like a painting.
A long street of Ming and Qing style shopfronts selling tea, ink stones, brushes and local crafts, a good place to stroll and sample snacks.
A walled town in the old Huizhou region, with stone archways, ancestral halls and narrow lanes that tell the story of the powerful Hui merchants.
Anhui's most famous dish: mandarin fish cured until it develops a strong smell, then braised or fried into tender, savory flesh. The smell is a warning but the taste is a delight.
Tofu left to grow a soft white fuzz of harmless mold, then pan-fried until crisp. Its flavor is savory and much milder than its look suggests.
A small, crisp, layered baked cake stuffed with preserved vegetables and pork, sold hot from clay ovens and a favorite Huangshan snack.
A prized green tea picked from the misty slopes of Huangshan, its slender leaves are tipped with white down and brew a fresh, sweet cup.
A layered stew pot that stacks meatballs, dumplings, ham, tofu and vegetables, traditionally served for family feasts and festivals.
Hui-style houses have white walls, grey tiled roofs, tall horse-head gables and richly carved wood, stone and brick that show a family's wealth.
Hui opera is an old regional opera. In the 18th century, Hui troupes came to Beijing, and their style helped shape Peking opera.
One of the four sacred mountains of Chinese Buddhism, dedicated to the bodhisattva Dizang. Temples dot its misty slopes, and pilgrims climb through incense and pines.
A hall at Jiuhua Mountain where the body of a revered monk was preserved. Pilgrims come to pay respect at this quiet, solemn place.
The mountain's temple kitchens make vegetarian dishes from tofu, mushrooms and local vegetables that are simple, wholesome and surprisingly tasty.
Huangjing is a root herb long used in Chinese medicine and food. It is grown on the cool slopes of Jiuhua and often steamed and sweetened.
Wuhu's small steamed buns have thin skins and a rich, juicy filling. They are a typical breakfast in this Yangtze river port.
A unique art invented in Wuhu, where blacksmiths forge thin iron strips into landscapes, flowers and birds that look like ink paintings.
A seven-story brick pagoda on the bank of the Yangtze in Anqing, built in the Ming dynasty to bring good fortune to the city.
A mountain of tall granite pillars and pines, called one of Anhui's finest. Its name means Heavenly Pillar Mountain.
A Buddhist temple beside the Yangtze in Anqing, with the Zhenfeng Pagoda close by. The two are often visited together.
A soft, sweet cake scented with osmanthus blossoms, a delicate local treat that goes well with a cup of tea.
One of the best-loved operas in China, with sweet, simple melodies and love stories. It grew from tea-picking songs near Anqing and is still performed across the country.
A crisp, flaky baked flatbread, often stuffed with meat or preserved vegetables and eaten fresh from the oven.
Big carp from the Huai River are stewed or braised in a rich, savory sauce. The dish is a staple of riverside meals.
A gentle hill near Huainan, wrapped in legends. It is best known as the supposed birthplace of tofu and as the site of a famous battle.
A walled town that still has its Song-dynasty city wall, among the best preserved in China. Locals say the wall has kept out floods for centuries.
Soft tofu made in the hills where, according to legend, it was first invented. Tofu here is steamed, fried and simmered in many ways.
A steaming beef broth that locals drink in the morning with a flatbread, spiced with pepper and coriander.
Fresh fish from the Yangtze at Caishiji, a cliff where the poet Li Bai is said to have died, is steamed or braised with local sauces.
Tongling is known for pale, tender ginger that is pickled or candied, and has been grown here for centuries.
A forest park high in the Dabie Mountains, with waterfalls, mossy rocks and cool air. It is a favorite summer escape.
One of China's famous teas, made from single leaves without stems or buds, rolled flat like melon seeds, with a fresh and mellow taste.
A rare yellow tea from the Huoshan hills. Its leaves are gently piled and slowly dried to give a soft, sweet flavor.
A well-known braised chicken, so tender that the meat falls off the bone. It has been a gift and a snack for travelers for generations.
A cold noodle dish of thick, chewy strips tossed in garlic, vinegar, chili and sesame sauce, popular in summer in Fuyang.
A soft steamed bread rolled around vegetables, egg or meat, a handy and filling breakfast in northern Anhui.
Salted, pressed and dried duck, steamed or boiled until tender and savory, a local specialty for the cold months.
A famous baijiu made in Bozhou with water from an ancient well. It was said to be offered as a tribute to emperors.
Bozhou is one of China's great herb trading centers, where markets stack roots, flowers and seeds used in traditional medicine.
A small pavilion in the hills of Chuzhou made famous by Ouyang Xiu's essay, in which a drunken old man finds joy in the mountains, not in wine.
Chuzhou's mountain cooking features wild vegetables, bamboo shoots, river fish and simple, hearty stews.
A street barbecue of skewered meat and vegetables, grilled over charcoal, and a lively evening tradition in northern Anhui.
